Thought: First, I need to understand what 2-methylpentan-2-ol looks like. It's a tertiary alcohol with the structure:
CH3-C(OH)(CH3)-CH2-CH2-CH3
This is a 5-carbon chain (pentane) with a tertiary alcohol at C2, and a methyl group also at C2.

Let me analyze each option:

A. Ethyl 2-methylbutanoate: This is CH3-CH(CH3)-CH2-C(=O)-OCH2CH3
   When reacted with CH3MgI, the Grignard attacks the carbonyl carbon, forming a tertiary alcohol after workup.
   The product would be CH3-CH(CH3)-CH2-C(OH)(CH3)-OCH2CH3, which is not 2-methylpentan-2-ol.

B. Ethyl butanoate: This is CH3-CH2-CH2-C(=O)-OCH2CH3
   When reacted with CH3MgI, the Grignard attacks the carbonyl carbon, forming a tertiary alcohol after workup.
   The product would be CH3-CH2-CH2-C(OH)(CH3)-OCH2CH3, which is not 2-methylpentan-2-ol.

C. Methyl propyl ketone: This is CH3-C(=O)-CH2-CH2-CH3
   When reacted with CH3MgI, the Grignard attacks the carbonyl carbon, forming a tertiary alcohol after workup.
   The product would be CH3-C(OH)(CH3)-CH2-CH2-CH3, which IS 2-methylpentan-2-ol.

D. Pentan-2-one: This is CH3-C(=O)-CH2-CH2-CH3
   This is the same as methyl propyl ketone, just named differently.
   When reacted with CH3MgI, the product would be CH3-C(OH)(CH3)-CH2-CH2-CH3, which IS 2-methylpentan-2-ol.

Looking at my analysis, options C and D both produce 2-methylpentan-2-ol. Options A and B produce different tertiary alcohols because they are esters, not ketones, and the resulting structure will contain an -OCH2CH3 group.
